Childhood leukemia survivors are at risk of long-term complications. Data on bone remodeling in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are limited. This 2-year prospective longitudinal study investigated bone remodeling and bone turnover markers at diagnosis, during treatment, and until stopping treatment, in ALL patients < 18 years, to clarify the influence of leukemia itself and/or chemotherapy on bone. Methods: A total of 22 ALL children (12 males, age 5.5 ± 3.6 years) underwent blood sampling at the 5 time point (T0−T4). Osteoprotegerin (OPG), receptor-activator-NF-B-ligand (RANKL), osteocalcin (OC), C-terminal-telopeptide-type-I-collagen (CTX), bone-alkaline-phosphatase (bALP), tartrate-resistant acid-phosphatase-5b (TRACP5b), procollagen-type-I-N-terminal-propeptide (P1NP), Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1), and sclerostin were assessed. Data from patients at T0 were compared to a control group of healthy children. We used the principal component analysis (PCA) for statistics. Results: Levels of CTX, OC, P1NP, and bALP resulted lower in ALL children than controls ( p = 0.009 for CTX and p < 0.001 for the others), also DKK1 and sclerostin ( p < 0.0001 and p = 0.023). RANKL ed OPG were higher in patients. During T0−T4, CTX, OC, P1NP, TRACP5b, and bALP showed a significant increase, in particular at T0−T1 (end-of-induction). Less evident changes were detected onwards. Conclusions: The onset of leukemia has been revealed as a key point in determining a slowing of bone remodeling in ALL children. acute lymhpoblastic leukemia (ALL) children bone remodeling bone turnover C-terminal-telopeptide-type-I-collagen (CTX) osteocalcin (OC) procollagen-type-I-N-terminal-propeptide (P1NP) This research received no external funding. 1. Introduction Improved results in the treatment of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), thanks to risk-adapted multiagent antileukemic therapy and supportive care, have led to about 90% of a 5-year survival rate [ 1 , 2 ]. However, the growing population of childhood leukemia survivors is at risk of long-term complications, due to the disease itself and to the treatment [ 3 ]. Drug exposure is the major determinant of late effects in childhood cancer survivors, including neurologic conditions [ 4 ], cardiometabolic alterations [ 5 , 6 , 7 ], and impact on skeletal mineralization [ 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Glucocorticoids (GCs) represent a key drug for the treatment of ALL, as both prednisone and dexamethasone, used during the induction and reinduction phases of treatment and in the consolidation phase of high-risk patients, have a crucial role. GCs promote apoptosis of osteoblasts and osteocytes and increase bone resorption, decreasing bone formation [ 11 , 12 ]. Furthermore, GCs influence the serum levels of calcium, reducing intestinal absorption and increasing renal excretion [ 13 ]. As a consequence, 30–50% of patients on chronic glucocorticoid (GC) therapy may present fractures [ 13 ]. Moreover cumulative doses of GCs have been related to the risk of osteonecrosis in patients with ALL, particularly in older ones, showing a slower clearance of drugs and subsequent increased bone toxicity [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. In adolescents suffering from ALL, important alterations of trabecular and cortical bone have been reported during the four-week induction treatment [ 20 ], while young adult survivors of pediatric ALL presented bone loss at the end of chemotherapy [ 21 ]. Moreover, osteoporosis and decreased bone mineral density (BMD) have been reported at the onset of childhood ALL, likely due to the action of autocrine factors linked to bone infiltration by malignant cells, indicating a direct effect of leukemic cells [ 22 , 23 ]. The possibility that leukemic B cells contribute directly to bone impairment has been explored in preclinical studies demonstrating a critical role of the receptor activator of the nuclear factor κB ligand (RANKL)-osteoprotegerin(OPG)/receptor activator of the nuclear factor κB (RANK) receptor axis in causing B-ALL cell-mediated bone damage [ 24 , 25 ]. All life long, the bone tissue has a continuous remodeling. The cells that promote bone remodeling are osteoclasts, the bone resorption cells, and osteoblasts, the bone-forming cells that lay down bone matrix proteins. The balance of bone remodeling is under control of the RANKL/OPG/RANK and Wnt/β-catenin pathways, which regulate osteoclastogenesis and osteoblastogenesis, respectively [ 26 , 27 ]. The Wnt/β-catenin pro-osteoblastogenic pathway can be inhibited by Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1) and sclerostin [ 28 ]. Pediatric bone diseases showed high serum levels of bone cytokines RANKL, sclerostin, and DKK-1. They also represent the target of emerging treatments for osteopenia and osteoporosis [ 29 ]. Markers of bone turnover reflect the activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts [ 30 ]. Namely, bone alkaline phosphatase (bALP) and osteocalcin (OC), a non-collagenous marker, and procollagen I N-propeptide (PINP), a collagenous marker, reflect osteoblast activity. On the other side, the production of type I collagen degradation fragments amino terminal telopeptides of type I collagen (NTX) and carbossi terminal telopeptides of type I collagen (CTX) and the enzyme tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase type 5b (TRAcP5b) represent markers of bone resorption [ 31 ]. RANKL/RANK/OPG and Wnt/β-catenin pathways, which control osteoclastogenesis and osteoblastogenesis, regulate this equilibrium [ 26 , 27 ]. Scarce are data describing bone remodeling in children and adolescents with ALL. Gupta et al. evaluated, in children with ALL, a bone resorption marker (CTX) at diagnosis and at the 3-month time point during treatment, reporting its increase during treatment [ 32 ]. Boot et al. found low lumbar spine bone mineral density and low markers of bone turnover in children with ALL at diagnosis, hypothesizing a role of leukemia itself on bone [ 33 ]. The alterations of the bone marrow microenvironment during leukemogenesis seem to lead to perturbed hematopoiesis, impaired B-lymphopoiesis, reduced production of collagen, and reduced number of osteoblasts. Leukemia cells produced high levels of RANKL, sufficient to cause osteoclast-mediated bone resorption [ 24 ]. Previously, we observed a biomarker signature of bone resorption in children and adolescents under intensive chemotherapy treatment for ALL [ 34 ]. In the present study, we investigated the changes in bone remodeling and bone turnover markers at the diagnosis, before any treatment, and through intensive phases of therapy until stopping treatment, in a cohort of children and adolescent with ALL. This prospective longitudinal study, with 2 years of follow-up, aimed at clarifying the influence of leukemia itself and/or the disease treatment on bone impairment.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Bone remodeling in children with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) and the impact of its treatment, including glucocorticoids, and related factors like vitamin D deficiency.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The onset of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) significantly slows bone remodeling in children, attributed to direct effects of leukemic cells, including infiltration of bone lacunae and release of autocrine factors. Specifically, leukemic B-cells contribute to bone impairment via the RANKL-OPG/RANK axis, leading to increased osteoclast activity and decreased osteoblastic cells, as evidenced by reduced osteocalcin mRNA. Alterations in the bone marrow microenvironment during leukemogenesis perturb hematopoiesis, impair B-lymphopoiesis, reduce collagen production, and decrease osteoblast numbers. Chemotherapy, particularly glucocorticoids (GCs), also plays a role by promoting osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis, increasing bone resorption, and decreasing bone formation, partly by influencing serum calcium levels. However, the transient nature of GC exposure in children with ALL often allows bone remodeling recovery, especially after the clearance of leukemic blasts. Beyond direct cellular effects, endothelial and cardiovascular damage can influence vascular damage to bone, contributing to osteonecrosis. Furthermore, factors like gut microbiome disruption can influence immune responses, leukemia progression, chronic inflammation, and overall bone health. A persistent issue observed is 25-OH-vitamin D deficiency, often due to deficient oral intake and lifestyle changes in children with leukemia.
related_biomarkers: Receptor activator of the nuclear factor κB (RANK)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The most significant changes in bone turnover markers, including CTX, OC, P1NP, TRACP5b, and bALP, were observed during the initial phase of treatment (T0-T1, end-of-induction), which coincided with the clearance of over 95% of bone marrow blasts. This suggests that the initial presence of leukemia is the primary driver of major bone changes, with less evident or no significant differences in marker profiles detected in later treatment phases (T1-T4). Cumulative doses of glucocorticoids (GCs) have been related to an increased risk of osteonecrosis, particularly in older patients due to slower drug clearance and increased bone toxicity. However, the study also found that different doses of GC did not exert any significant, different effect on the bone marker profile of children after intensive phases of leukemia therapy, and no imbalance of bone remodeling was documented after exposure to two phases of high-dose GC treatment.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study highlights that the onset of leukemia itself is a key determinant in slowing bone remodeling, with direct effects from leukemic cells through autocrine factors and the RANKL-OPG/RANK axis causing bone impairment. Specific alterations in trabecular and cortical bone are noted during the four-week induction treatment in adolescents with ALL. While glucocorticoids (GCs) contribute to bone impairment by promoting osteoblast/osteocyte apoptosis and increasing resorption, their exposure in children with ALL is often transient. This transient exposure appears to allow for bone remodeling recovery, particularly in growing children, and the study found that chemotherapy and GCs did not exacerbate bone impairment beyond what is generally reported, consistent with an intermittent GC exposure model.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Children and adolescents with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) (patients < 18 years, specifically 1-18 years with a mean age of 5.5 ";" 3.6 years), including childhood leukemia survivors and young adult survivors of pediatric ALL.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) intrinsically impairs bone metabolism, leading to significantly lower levels of bone formation and resorption markers at diagnosis compared to healthy children. This results in a general slowing of bone remodeling and a risk of long-term skeletal complications, including osteoporosis, decreased bone mineral density (BMD), fractures (reported in 30-50% of patients on chronic glucocorticoid therapy), and osteonecrosis (severe osteonecrosis reported in 4.5% of the studied cohort). Bone pain was also reported in 22.7% of patients. Beyond bone health, patients are at risk for other long-term complications like neurologic conditions and cardiometabolic alterations. However, bone remodeling can recover in growing children with ALL after transient glucocorticoid exposure, and evaluation of skeletal health status at diagnosis is crucial. Furthermore, insufficient or deficient 25-OH-vitamin D is widely reported in children with leukemia, warranting supplementation for optimal bone health.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: There is an adverse risk for long-term complications affecting bone health, including skeletal mineralization issues, fractures, osteonecrosis, and a general slowing of bone remodeling, primarily due to the intrinsic effects of leukemia. However, there is also a management utility or protective benefit for skeletal health, as bone remodeling can recover in growing children with transient glucocorticoid exposure. The study suggests potential diagnostic utility for early detection of bone involvement in ALL, based on significant changes observed at diagnosis, and that rapid changes from T0 to T1 could serve as a monitoring tool for treatment response and bone recovery.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: C-terminal-telopeptide-type-I-collagen (CTX), Osteocalcin (OC), and Procollagen-type-I-N-terminal-propeptide (P1NP) were identified as highly reliable biomarkers, explaining over 60% of the variance in bone remodeling over time. Bone-alkaline-phosphatase (bALP), Parathyroid hormone (PTH), and 25-OH-vitamin D also explained approximately 50% of the variance, with all these key variables showing strong statistical significance in ANOVA on repeated measures. The study notes that the transient nature of glucocorticoid (GC) exposure in children with ALL allows for bone remodeling recovery, explaining the limited impact of GCs on bone remodeling in different treatment phases and supporting the dynamic of bone health recovery once leukemic blasts are cleared. The overall panel of bone turnover markers (OPG, RANKL, OC, CTX, bALP, TRACP5b, P1NP, DKK-1, sclerostin) used for investigation suggests their established utility in assessing bone remodeling.
